newsitem.title: USA: Moody's gives U.S. debt top rating.
newsitem.headline: Moody's gives U.S. debt top rating.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service Inc. Thursday gave the United States -- the world's largest economy -- a top credit rating, and you can take it to the bank.
The firm confirmed the "Aaa" rating on U.S. debt, which will hold down the cost of financing the nation's debt load.
"Moody's Investors Service finds the credit rating of the debt of the United States of America is still solidly Aaa, despite some credit concerns," the rating agency said in a statement.
The concerns are related primarily to the nation's hefty upcoming medical and pension costs associated with an ageing population, Moody's said.

But the rating agency said the concerns are far outweighed by the "size and depth of the U.S. economy, underlying political consensus, and the dominant role that the country plays in the world's major economic and political forums."

In its first in-depth credit report on the United States, Moody's said that "when combined with comparatively low debt levels and with an intermediate-term outlook for relatively strong economic growth and low inflation, these strengths indicate very low risk of a default on U.S. Treasury bonds."

Moody's said it produced the report in response to increased investor demand for in-depth analysis on G-5 nations, the world's biggest industrialised countries -- Germany, Japan, France, Britain and the United States.

"Although Moody's has maintained a triple-A rating on debt of the United States since World War I, investor demand for in-depth analysis on the U.S. is a new phenomenon," said Christopher Mahoney, managing director of Moody's banking and sovereign ratings group.

That demand is being driven mainly by the concerns of overseas bond investors over the potential credit risks stemming from the U.S. budget deficit and its sizable current account deficits, Moody's said.

When the debt ceiling debate threatened interest payments and some principal payments on U.S. Treasury obligations in 1996, Moody's placed its Aaa rating on $300 billion of U.S. Treasury bonds under review for possible downgrade.

"Moody's will continue to monitor the underlying debate over the size and role of the United States government to determine if meeting the full-faith-and-credit obligations of the country could once again be at risk as a result of policy disagreements between the legislative and executive branches," it said.
Last week, the Senate approved a five-year balanced budget plan, worked out between the White House and Congress.
The budget plan trims Medicare by $115 billion over five years and makes changes that are expected to keep it solvent for the next decade.

Recent improvement in federal government finances provides evidence that the United States will be able to keep its debt burden at manageable levels over the long term, Moody's said. Last year's budget deficit came in at $107 billion, down from $164 billion in 1995. "The rating agency expects that the deficit will continue to improve in 1997," it said.
